01 · The audit — caught before Satoshi, not after

The random-cohort claim was wrong on all three counts — and was never comparable anyway.

The deck, PHASE3_SUMMARY.md and the draft email all said the low-OC/EC cohort "beats ten size-matched random cohorts, RMSE 3.4 vs 4.4–7.3" on held-out TOR. run_ftir_11.py:55 sets five controls, not ten; the committed held-out table runs 3.10–5.00, not 4.4–7.3; and random 800 #3 comes in at 3.097, beating the selected cohort's 3.415 outright. This answers your July question — why is the intercept negative when nothing at Addis is. Set predicted EC to zero and the intercept becomes a quantity you can go looking for: 18.8–26.1 Mm⁻¹, median 21.5, about 46% of the median Addis Fabs of 47.11. Slopes span 3.4× across those six setups and intercepts 4.3×; C spans 1.4×. And C is exactly MAC-invariant by construction, so the target is well posed whether or not the MAC fork is ever settled.

The caveat, before you raise it. C is invariant to any multiplicative rescaling of the predicted-EC axis — changing MAC is exactly that, and changing training cohort largely is too. So these are not six independent routes converging on 21 Mm⁻¹. The honest claim is "the additive offset is robust to every scaling choice we have made", not "six methods agree".

New overnight, and it is the sharpest cheap test we had. AIRSpec touches only the spectra and never Fabs, yet it halves the intercept, −3.2215 → −1.6151 — which looks like a refutation of "the offset is in x". It is not, because it also halves the slope, and under y = a(x − c) the intercept is −a·c. A y-side gain change must move the intercept in proportion to the slope and leave c alone. It does: slope ratio 0.5406 against intercept ratio 0.5013, and c moves −7.3% where a and b each move ~50%.

This is the answer to your July question — why is the intercept negative when nothing at Addis is. Set predicted EC to zero and the intercept stops being a regression artifact and becomes a quantity you could go and look for: about twenty-one inverse megametres of absorption at the HIPS wavelength with no FTIR-EC behind it. That is forty-six percent of a typical Addis filter.

Across all six calibration setups it runs eighteen-point-eight to twenty-six, median twenty-one-and-a-half, while the slopes across those same six span three-and-a-half fold. And it is exactly MAC-invariant by construction, so the target is well posed whether or not the MAC fork is ever settled.

Now the caveat, before you get to it. C is invariant to any multiplicative rescaling of the EC axis. Changing MAC is exactly that, and changing training cohort mostly is. So these are not six independent routes agreeing. The honest claim is that the additive offset is robust to every scaling choice we have made — not that six methods corroborate each other.

One thing that did land overnight, and it is the sharpest cheap test we had. AIRSpec touches only the spectra, never Fabs, and it halves the intercept. That looks like a refutation of "the offset lives in x". It is not, because it also halves the slope — and under y equals a times x minus c, the intercept is minus a times c. Slope ratio 0.54, intercept ratio 0.50, and c moves seven percent where a and b each move fifty.

If she pushes on "so what does it license": nothing about the cause. C is a restatement of the intercept, not new evidence about where it comes from. Brown carbon, dust, a HIPS-generic offset and an FTIR zero error are all still live on this slide alone — slides 04 and 05 are what start eliminating them.

If she pushes on the −7.3%: it is systematic, not noise. Across the six setups c runs 1.885 to 2.608 and the best-performing setup has the lowest c. A single shared c fitted jointly costs only 1.6% in total RSS. But that agreement is confounded by the same gain-invariance, so it corroborates rather than proves.

04 · Result — is it a generic HIPS zero?committed · ftir_26 (0088e05)

No. IMPROVE HIPS runs through the origin — which makes the offset Addis-specific, and leaves two explanations that are not an absorber.

ftir_16 · improve_implied_mac_curveThe same 151,843-filter HIPS↔TOR join the new fits run through; the reproduction gate matched ftir_16's committed values

Attack-plan Tier 1, item 1, answered: regress IMPROVE Fabs on TOR EC and read the intercept in Mm⁻¹. Pooled OLS gives +1.345 [+1.195, +1.485]; trim the top 5% of EC and it falls to +0.200; in the Addis-like OC/EC ≤ 2.27 subset, trimmed, +0.097 [−0.034, +0.218] — the site-cluster interval, which includes zero; the tighter [+0.069, +0.124] is i.i.d.-row and ~4× too optimistic here. At EC ≤ 0 (n = 4,247) the median Fabs is +0.12 Mm⁻¹ with 23.8% of filters reading negative — zero at zero, with symmetric noise. Per site, 170 of 176 are "significantly" nonzero by OLS, but that is n-power, not magnitude: no site reaches 5 Mm⁻¹ (max 4.64). And the arithmetic killer — only 186 of 160,023 IMPROVE filters (0.12%) carry 21.5 Mm⁻¹ of total absorption, so a generic 21.5 Mm⁻¹ zero-offset is not a thing that could exist. Upper bound ~1.3 Mm⁻¹, i.e. 6% of C; the defensible number is 0.1–0.25, ≤ 1%.

The counterweight, and it is real. Two explanations survive this, and neither is an absorber. (i) Curvature. Fabs is concave in EC — Fabs = 7.50·EC^0.796, R² 0.713, passing through zero — and fitting a straight line to a concave relation manufactures a negative intercept with no offset present. Per-site intercepts run at a median 35% of site mean Fabs (IQR 27–50%); Addis is 21.5/47.11 = 46%, and 32% of IMPROVE sites show a fraction at or above Addis's — in data whose true offset at zero is ~0. (ii) A loading-dependent HIPS artifact. IMPROVE's median Fabs is 1.26 Mm⁻¹ against Addis's 47.11, a 37× gap: this rules out an additive, loading-independent offset but says nothing about one that grows with loading. Per-site intercept does grow with loading (r = 0.689), and extrapolating to Fabs = 47.11 gives 16.2 Mm⁻¹ — 75% of C — six times beyond IMPROVE's largest site median of 8.1, so this analysis cannot close it either way.

And separating those three needs a reference we do not have. Both candidate EC references in the committed dataset turn out to be circular, one on each axis. ChemSpec_BC is Fabs/10 rounded to 2 dp — R² 0.9982, implied MAC 10.0003 — so it is circular with x. ChemSpec_EC was written up in ftir_25 as the independent one; it is not. Against EC_ftir at ETAD: n = 175, r² = 0.999693, ratio median 1.0000 (IQR 0.999–1.001), median |difference| 0.0030 µg/m³ — exactly the 2-dp rounding half-width. It is FTIR-EC itself, rounded, arriving through SPARTAN's speciation table, and docs/open-items.md has flagged the same thing in the four-sites data for weeks. The tell was already in the numbers we quoted — its R² of 0.79 against Fabs matches FTIR-EC's own 0.76 because it is FTIR-EC — and it was read as corroboration. ftir_25 has been corrected and pushed (00ab987).

What that costs us, and what it buys. "Go find ~21 Mm⁻¹ of brown carbon" is materially weaker as a framing than it was yesterday morning — you should hear that today rather than after Satoshi does. But the argument that replaces it is cleaner: the offset is not a generic HIPS zero, it is not on the FTIR axis, the MA350 cannot see whether it is BrC, and nothing in hand can discriminate the three survivors because every candidate reference is circular with one axis or the other. That is not a gap in the story — it is the case for the quartz-TOR campaign, made from four directions.

Speaker notes

Tier-1 item one came back. The question was whether HIPS generically reads a few inverse megametres at zero EC — filter scattering, the tau-to-Fabs conversion, loading correction. If it does, part of our offset is instrument-generic. It does not. Regress IMPROVE Fabs on TOR EC across the hundred-and-fifty-thousand-filter join and the intercept is one-point-three pooled, nought-point-two trimmed, and nought-point-one in the Addis-like subset. At EC at or below zero the median Fabs is plus nought-point-one-two, with twenty-four percent of filters reading negative — that is zero at zero with symmetric noise. No individual site reaches five. And the arithmetic that settles it: only a hundred and eighty-six IMPROVE filters out of a hundred and sixty thousand carry twenty-one megametres of total absorption. A generic offset that size is not a thing that could exist.

So the offset is Addis-specific. Now the part that cuts the other way, and I want you to hear it today rather than tomorrow.

Two explanations survive this, and neither one is an absorber. The first is curvature. Fabs is concave in EC across IMPROVE — it goes as EC to the nought-point-eight, passing exactly through zero — and fitting a straight line to a concave relationship manufactures a negative intercept with no offset present at all. Per-site intercepts run at a median thirty-five percent of site mean Fabs. Addis is forty-six percent. A third of IMPROVE sites show a fraction at or above Addis's — in data where the true offset at zero is zero.

The second is a loading-dependent HIPS artifact. IMPROVE's median Fabs is one-point-three against Addis's forty-seven — a thirty-seven-fold gap. That gap cleanly rules out an additive, loading-independent offset. It says nothing about one that grows with loading. And per-site intercept does grow with loading; extrapolate to Addis loading and you get sixteen megametres, three-quarters of our C. That extrapolation is six times beyond IMPROVE's largest site, so it does not close the question either — but it means I cannot rule it out.

And separating those three needs a reference we do not have. Both ChemSpec columns are circular. BC is Fabs over ten, rounded — circular with x. EC I wrote up in ftir_25 as the independent one, and this morning I disproved that: against FTIR-EC it is r-squared nought-point-nine-nine-nine-seven, ratio one-point-zero-zero-zero-zero, median difference three thousandths of a microgram, which is exactly the two-decimal rounding half-width. It is our own FTIR-EC coming back through the speciation table. The tell was already in the numbers I had quoted — its R-squared against Fabs matches FTIR-EC's own, because it is FTIR-EC — and I read it as corroboration. ftir_25 is corrected and pushed.

Which means: "go find twenty-one megametres of brown carbon" is a materially weaker framing than it was yesterday. But what replaces it is cleaner — not a generic HIPS zero, not on the FTIR axis, the MA350 cannot see it, and nothing in hand can discriminate what is left. That is the case for quartz TOR, made from four directions.

This is the slide to give the most air. It is both the strongest support for the story and its sharpest caveat, and she should hear the caveat from you rather than infer it.

If she pushes on the concavity number: the 0.796 exponent is itself attenuated by the same errors-in-variables problem, so treat it as an upper bound on how concave the relationship really is — which makes it an upper bound on how much of our intercept curvature could explain.

If she asks whether we can test curvature on Addis directly: not right now. It needs an EC reference that is derived from neither Fabs nor FTIR, and after this morning there is no such column in the committed dataset. It waits on quartz TOR like everything else.

If she asks why 170 of 176 sites are "significant": that is n-power, not magnitude. The sites have thousands of filters each. Magnitude is the number that matters and no site reaches five.

Methodological aside, only if she asks about estimator choice: the pooled intercept is monotone increasing in lambda, so OLS is the maximum over all errors-in-variables lambdas.

Every EIV correction moves it toward zero. That makes the OLS column a hard upper bound rather than a point estimate, which is why the "≤ 1%" claim is safe.

This was the single most decisive analysis available without new sampling, and it is closed. Attributing the 625-nm excess over an AAE_BC ≈ 1 anchor at 880 gives a negative brown-carbon absorption on most days, and closing the ~21 Mm⁻¹ gap would need AAE_BC = 0.316, which no combustion aerosol has. But the instrument-health check says why: on MA350-0238 the Green channel implies a negative AAE, UV is out of range on a third of days, and Red sits on top of IR to within channel reproducibility. The sentence to use, in the deck and in the room, is "the MA350 cannot answer this question." That is a statement about the instrument, not about the air: nothing here bounds how much brown carbon Addis actually has, and the negative-sounding version of this result is not one we can support.

Two live repo traps got fixed on the way through, and both are committed (3aedfdc). processed_sites/README.md documented AE33 wavelengths (370/520/660) over what are actually five-channel MA350 exports (375/470/528/625/880) — the first file a reader meets. And optics.aae_from_columns defaults to kind='BCc', which is offset from the atmospheric AAE by an exact identity: −1.0157 for UV/IR and −0.9674 for Red/IR on the MA350 firmware constants. On the Addis instrument that reads AAE(Red,IR) as −0.024 where absorption gives 0.943 — and through classify_aae it turned 47% biomass into 12%.

This was the single most decisive analysis available without new sampling, and it is closed — but not the way we wanted. Anchor AAE_BC at one on the 880 channel, attribute the excess at 625 to brown carbon, and you get a negative brown-carbon absorption on eighty-five percent of days. Closing our twenty-one-megametre gap would need an AAE for black carbon of nought-point-three-two, which no combustion aerosol has.

The instrument health check says why. On this instrument the Green channel implies a negative AAE, which is unphysical. UV is out of range on a third of days. And Red sits on top of IR to within channel reproducibility. Only the IR channel is trustworthy — and IR is precisely the channel that carries no brown-carbon information.

So the sentence is: the MA350 cannot answer this question. That is a statement about the instrument, not about the air.

07 · Resolved this morning — the HIPS wavelengthresolved · SPARTAN sources

HIPS is the He–Ne line: 632.8 ≈ 633 nm — and MAC 10 belongs to 633.

The 405-vs-633 question closed itself: SPARTAN's Instruments page says the filters are illuminated with a HeNe laser (632 nm) — and notes the HIPS analysis is performed by your group at UC Davis — while the 2025 SPARTAN methods paper states He–Ne at 633 nm and uses MAC = 10 m²/g at 633 nm. IMPROVE literature likewise reports 633. The 632/633 spread is rounding of the 632.8 nm He–Ne line. RESEARCH_PROGRESS.md's 405 was wrong and is corrected in this commit, along with the optics reference's OPEN cells.

Three consequences. ① The AERONET dust null was aimed at the right wavelength after all — and dust absorbs less at 633 than at 405, so that null strengthens, narrowing "real non-EC absorption" toward brown carbon specifically. ② The MA350's Red channel (625 nm) sits essentially at the HIPS wavelength, so slide 06's no-red-excess result bears directly on the band HIPS measures — within the limits of a channel that cannot resolve small excesses. ③ Classic BrC absorbs weakly at 633, so among the three surviving explanations, "real non-EC absorption" loses weight unless the absorber is char/tar-like; the loading-dependent artifact and curve geometry gain correspondingly. None of this moves the headline ask — quartz TOR separates the survivors at any wavelength.

What remains is semantics, not existence. At ETAD, HIPS_Uncertainty and HIPS_MDL exist as their own Parameter rows — not as the Uncertainty column on HIPS_Fabs rows (0/190), which is why AGENTS.md said "unpopulated". HIPS_Uncertainty is 190/190 at median 2.9075 Mm⁻¹ (6.17% of median Fabs), giving Deming λ* ≈ 2.96 — and λ=1 overstates the errors-in-variables intercept correction by ~55%. The ask for SPARTAN: is that field counting statistics, repeatability, or propagated calibration uncertainty? Only the last two make λ* defensible as a measurement error.

Before building the notebook, here is what the committed residual table already says. For the raw model the per-season mean residual is Dry −1.25 — the worst — Belg −0.47, and Kiremt +0.49, the nearest to zero. That is the opposite way round from "the dry, diesel-leaning aerosol is roughly right and the wet, charcoal-dominated seasons break". For the corrected model the residuals are season-stable: −2.59 Dry, −2.32 Belg, −2.04 Kiremt. So season sensitivity is a raw-model phenomenon, which is itself the interesting result — and it is consistent with the corrected model's error being a constant rather than a domain failure.

The confound to design around. Dry spans only about 55% of the wet seasons' x-range, so a naive per-season slope is mechanically attenuated: a shorter segment of the same line looks like a different line. The notebook has to be a pooled fit with a season × x interaction, not three separate crossplots, or it will find a seasonal effect whether or not one exists.

R2 · July slide 23 — the burning signature

Charring converts O–H and aliphatic C–H into aromatic C=C at ~1600 — the process argument for the Addis band.

July-17 deck · slide 23 (McCall series)Δ SNV absorbance, char minus unburned feedstock; low-temp 150–350 °C, high-temp 400–700 °C

Never walked through in July. Burning removes O–H (~3300) and aliphatic C–H (~2920) and grows aromatic C=C at exactly the 1600 band — more strongly at higher pyrolysis temperature. That is a process-based reason to read the Addis 1600 band as aromatic, not just a correlation. Honesty note for the room: char peaks near 1590–1600; Addis sits at 1617–1619 — charcoal-consistent, not charcoal-matched. The sub-1425 region is greyed because PTFE dominates it on Addis filters — which is exactly why the sub-1500 model ask to Satoshi matters.
